text:
Five papers shaped the current measurements and glyph-selection workflow. The 2017 systematic review informs the later study-design phase.
Legg et al. support pairwise and set-relative perceptual distance; clustering is a project step applied afterward, not a method validated by that paper.
The stated research gap is limited to the reviewed local literature: this corpus does not establish validated size-dependent thresholds for heterogeneous icon sets.
Maguire et al. (2012) was reviewed as design context but is omitted from the main narrative because it did not materially determine the current image-feature implementation.

text:
This slide separates three outcomes that should not be collapsed into one measure.

Fuchs et al. (2014), Experiment 2: 62 Amazon Mechanical Turk workers were accepted; 36 were retained after three control questions. Each participant completed 48 trials. A highlighted target appeared with eight alternatives in a 3×3 arrangement, and the participant selected the most similar glyph without training or an explanation of the encoded data.

Legg et al. (2017 issue; copyright 2016): 20 University of Oxford students or employees were recruited and one outlier was excluded. Participants rated 104 glyph pairs on an integer 0–10 scale according to how well they could differentiate them; the 96 non-reference pairs were randomized.

Fuchs et al. (2017): the systematic review synthesized 64 quantitative controlled data-glyph user-study papers. Accuracy was recorded in 63 of 64, completion time in 42, and qualitative feedback in 19. The authors also warn that participant preference did not always match measured performance.

Boundary for this thesis: these sources support similarity choice, pairwise differentiation, and task-performance measures. They do not directly establish semantic identification thresholds for heterogeneous icons at reduced sizes.
